newsitem.title: CHINA: EU's Brittan says may push China's WTO bid.
newsitem.headline: EU's Brittan says may push China's WTO bid.

text.p: European Commission Vice-President Sir Leon Brittan said on Thursday he might soon urge the United States to move quickly on China's long-stalled plan to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
He said that if Chinese leaders reaffirmed their commitment to a long-held European position on WTO, he would then press the case with the United States.
"I will certainly take up the matter with the Americans with extreme urgency...urging them that the time has come to adopt the approach that Europe has pioneered," he told a business conference.
"Recent stirrings in the media...suggest that the U.S. is perhaps readier now than over the past two years to heed European calls for decisive engagement on this negotiation," Brittan said.
China and many of its major trade partners have long disagreed over the terms of admission for China into the WTO.
Beijing has said it should be admitted under the more lenient rules for developing countries, while the United States has insisted that the Chinese economy was too big for such treatment.

Europe has maintained that it would be flexible on requirements for China's full implementation of WTO rules. But Beijing had to make clear its commitment to full compliance and show substantial initial movement on granting access to its domestic markets.

Brittan, who is leading a delegation of 30 European business leaders hoping to tap into the Chinese market, said he would meet senior Chinese officials, including Vice Premier Zhu Rongji and Minister of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation Wu Yi.
Chinese leaders appeared to have expected little progress until the U.S. presidential elections were over, Brittan said.
The end of the election campaign and the re-election of President Bill Clinton could now mean a new opportunity for the negotiating parties to move ahead on the WTO issue.
"I hope even before the end of this visit to be able to announce some specific action" in advancing the process, he said.
On Wednesday, Chinese leaders denounced Beijing's exclusion from the WTO as unjust, saying the world's largest developing nation had made great strides in opening its markets to trade and investment.
